title: Book cost and carrying value belong in the same table
content:
Most treasury packs lead with one number. Either the book shows what the company paid, which is stable and reconciles to the ledger, or it shows what the holdings are worth now, which is the number people actually ask about. Showing one without the other invites the wrong conversation.

What each number answers

Book cost answers an accounting question: what did the company commit, and against which approval. It does not move with the market, which is exactly why it is the right anchor for a reconciliation.

Carrying value answers a position question: if the board asked today what the holdings are worth, what is the answer. It moves constantly, and on its own it tells you nothing about whether a position has performed.

Why the pair matters

The gap between them is the unrealised result, and that is the only figure that says anything about the decision. A line carrying at $1.6m means little. A line that cost $1.4m and carries at $1.6m is a different statement, and one the treasurer can speak to.

Showing both also makes a common error visible. When someone quotes a return that looks too good, it is usually because the denominator has quietly become carrying value rather than book cost. Two columns side by side make that hard to do by accident.

A practical layout

  • Book cost and carrying value as adjacent columns, not separate schedules
  • The unrealised result in both dollars and percent, because the percent hides size and the dollar figure hides proportion
  • A total row that actually sums the lines above it

None of this is sophisticated. It is simply harder to do by hand each month than it looks, which is why the workbook usually ends up showing whichever number was easiest to refresh.

PortfolioHQ sets out both from the custodian file you already receive. Nothing here is a valuation for statutory accounts.

title: Reading issuer concentration before it reaches the committee
content:
Concentration is rarely discovered. It is usually noticed late, by someone preparing a paper, at the point where it is awkward to raise.

Line count is not diversification

A book with thirty lines can be more concentrated than one with twelve. What matters is how carrying value is distributed, not how many entries the schedule has. A single holding at nineteen percent of the book is a different risk from nineteen holdings at one percent each, and a line count treats them identically.

Sort by value, every time

The single most useful view of a treasury book is its holdings ranked by carrying value, largest first, with each line's share of the total beside it. It takes seconds to read and it answers the question a committee will ask.

Two things usually become obvious:

  • The top three lines account for more of the book than anyone had assumed
  • The largest position is often not the one people name when asked

Check it on every refresh, not every quarter

Concentration does not arrive in a single decision. It accumulates through a run of individually reasonable ones, each of which was fine on its own terms. Measuring only at quarter end means the first time anyone sees the drift is in the same meeting where they have to explain it.

Measuring on every upload costs nothing once the report is automatic, and it changes the conversation from explaining a breach to flagging an approach to one.

Say what the limit is

A concentration figure without a policy limit beside it is just trivia. If the investment policy says no single issuer above ten percent, the report should make it obvious which lines are near that, not leave the reader to do arithmetic.

PortfolioHQ ranks holdings by carrying value and shows each line's share of the book. It does not know your policy limits, so the comparison is still yours to make.

title: What a holdings statement cannot tell you
content:
It is worth being precise about the limits of a management report, because the gap between what it shows and what people assume it shows is where mistakes live.

It is not a valuation for the accounts

A holdings statement built from a custodian export is a management view. It is not prepared under an accounting standard, it has not been reviewed, and it should never be lifted into statutory reporting. The figures may agree. That is not the same as being the same thing.

It describes one file at one moment

Every figure traces back to the export that was uploaded and the valuation date on it. If that file is a week old, the report is a week old, however current it looks on screen. Nothing refreshes in the background.

It does not know about costs

Custody fees, FX on settlement, and transaction costs rarely appear in a holdings export, which means they rarely appear in the report. A gain quoted before costs is not the gain that reached the company. For small positions the difference is noise; for a large rebalance it is not.

It does not know your policy

The report can tell you that one issuer is nineteen percent of the book. It cannot tell you whether that breaches anything, because it has never seen the investment policy. That judgement stays with the treasurer.

It is not a book of record

The ledger is the book of record. A reporting tool sits beside it and should be reconciled to it, not trusted over it.

What it is good for

  • Seeing the shape of the book without rebuilding a workbook each month
  • Noticing drift between formal reviews
  • Giving the finance team one artefact to circulate rather than four versions of a spreadsheet

Used for that, it earns its place. Used as a valuation, it does not.

title: How a compliant book goes offside without a decision
content:
Policy breaches are usually imagined as an event: somebody buys something they should not have. In practice the more common route is quieter, and nobody does anything wrong at all.

Drift, not decisions

Suppose the policy caps technology at twenty-five percent of the book. At the start of the year the sector sits at nineteen. Nobody buys another technology name all year. By December the sector is at twenty-seven percent, because those holdings appreciated faster than the rest of the book.

No decision caused that. No approval was skipped. The weighting moved because weightings are a ratio, and the denominator changed.

Why it goes unnoticed

Sector weighting is usually calculated at review points, because calculating it by hand is tedious. Between reviews the book is assumed to be where it was left. That assumption holds for line items and fails for percentages.

The same mechanism works in reverse and is even easier to miss. A sector can fall below a policy minimum because everything else rose.

What to do about it

  • Recalculate exposure on every refresh, not on a review calendar
  • Look at the direction of travel, not just the current figure — a sector at twenty-two percent and rising is more interesting than one at twenty-four and flat
  • Write down the date a weighting was last inside the limit, not just whether it is inside today

Raise it early

A weighting approaching a limit is a routine note. The same weighting discovered past the limit, three months after it crossed, is an incident. The difference is entirely in when somebody looked.

PortfolioHQ recalculates sector exposure every time a file is uploaded, which makes the drift visible between formal reviews rather than at them.

title: Your custodian export is already the right starting point
content:
Finance teams often assume that getting holdings into a reporting tool means an integration, a project, and a conversation with IT. For a reporting view, it usually does not.

The file already exists

Custodians and brokers send holdings files already, on a schedule somebody has already agreed. That file has been reconciled, it comes from the counterparty of record, and it arrives without anyone having to ask. It is a better starting point than a credential-based integration for the simple reason that it is already trusted.

What a reporting view actually needs

Less than people expect. A symbol and a quantity per line is the minimum. Cost basis, current price, sector and asset type are read where present and ignored where not.

What it does not need is equally worth stating: no account numbers, no counterparty references, no signatory details, and no login to anything. A tool that reports on holdings has no business holding credentials to the account those holdings sit in.

Column names do not have to match

Reporting formats differ by custodian and nobody wants to maintain a mapping sheet. Headings are matched flexibly — Symbol or Ticker, Quantity or Shares — so an existing report format usually works untouched.

The trade-off to be clear about

Working from a file rather than a connection means nothing updates on its own. The report reflects the export it was built from and the valuation date on it. Refreshing means uploading a newer file.

For month-end reporting that is a reasonable trade: no integration to maintain, no credentials in circulation, and a report that is explicitly as current as the file behind it. For intraday position monitoring it is the wrong tool, and it is better to say so.

title: The note nobody writes
content:
Every position was bought for a reason. Within a year, that reason exists only in somebody's memory, and within two it usually does not exist at all.

How the knowledge leaves

The decision is taken once, under conditions that will not repeat. It is minuted, perhaps, in a form that records the approval rather than the thinking. Then the person who held the context moves team, and what remains on the schedule is a line with a quantity and a cost.

At the next review, somebody asks why the company holds it. The honest answer is that nobody remembers, so the position persists by default. Inertia is not a strategy, but it is what you get when the rationale is not written down.

What is worth recording

Less than a memo, more than nothing. Three sentences against each line usually covers it:

  • What the position is for — liquidity, yield, a strategic holding, a legacy from an acquisition
  • What would make the company exit it
  • Anything unusual about how it was acquired or how it is valued

The second one is the one people skip and the one that matters most at review.

Keep it with the numbers

A rationale filed separately from the holdings schedule is a rationale nobody reads. The value comes from it being in the same artefact as the figures, so that reading the line and reading the reason are the same action.

It is cheapest at the time

Writing three sentences when the position is opened costs a few minutes. Reconstructing the same three sentences two years later costs an afternoon, several emails, and usually produces a worse answer.

PortfolioHQ keeps internal notes against the statement. They stay internal unless somebody chooses to publish them.

title: One file, one moment: valuation date discipline
content:
A holdings report carries an implicit claim: that every figure in it describes the same instant. It is surprisingly easy to break that claim, and surprisingly hard to notice once broken.

How mixed dates happen

Somebody refreshes part of a workbook. A price is updated for the line being discussed but not for the rest. Two custodian files with different valuation dates get combined because both were in the folder. None of this is careless; it is what happens when a report is assembled by hand under time pressure.

The result is a total that corresponds to no actual moment. It is not wrong in any single cell, which is why review rarely catches it.

Make the date explicit

The simplest defence is to state the valuation date on the report itself, prominently, and to make it a property of the whole document rather than a footnote. A reader who can see that the statement is dated the twenty-eighth will ask the right question if it is now the fifteenth of the following month.

One source per statement

Build the report from one file. If two custodians are involved, either reconcile them to a common date first or produce two statements and say so. Averaging across dates to get a single number is how a book acquires figures nobody can reproduce.

Re-upload rather than patch

When something looks stale, the instinct is to correct the stale line. The better move is to produce a fresh export and rebuild the whole statement from it. It takes about the same time and the result has an unambiguous date.

PortfolioHQ builds every statement from a single uploaded file and reports the figures in it. Correcting a statement means uploading a newer export, not editing the one on screen.

title: Counterparty and issuer are two different concentrations
content:
These get used interchangeably in conversation, and the difference matters as soon as something goes wrong.

Issuer concentration

Issuer concentration asks: how much of the book depends on one company's fortunes. If the company holds a large position in a single name, that is issuer risk, and it is what a ranked holdings schedule shows.

Counterparty concentration

Counterparty concentration asks a different question: how much of the book sits with one institution. A portfolio spread across twenty issuers but held entirely at one custodian or executed through one broker is diversified by issuer and concentrated by counterparty.

The two can look identical on a holdings schedule, because a holdings export typically lists what is held and not where it is held.

Why the distinction bites

They fail differently. Issuer risk shows up as a valuation move you can see in the report. Counterparty risk shows up as an operational problem — access, settlement, or recovery — and it does not appear in a carrying value at all until it is acute.

A report built from a single custodian export is, by construction, blind to the second one. It can only describe the holdings in the file it was given.

What to do

  • Track counterparty exposure separately, from the custodian relationships rather than from the holdings schedule
  • Do not let a well-diversified issuer table stand in for a counterparty answer
  • Say explicitly, in the pack, which of the two a given table is describing

PortfolioHQ reports issuer concentration from the uploaded file. It has no view of where those holdings are custodied, and should not be read as covering counterparty exposure.

title: Preparing the treasury section of a board pack
content:
The treasury section is usually short, read quickly, and asked about precisely. Writing it for that reality helps.

Lead with the position, not the activity

Boards want to know where the company stands before they want to know what the team did. Open with book cost, carrying value and the unrealised result. Activity during the period belongs after that, not before it.

Three figures carry most of the meaning

  • Carrying value, with the valuation date beside it
  • The unrealised result in dollars and percent
  • The largest single holding as a share of the book

If the section said only these three things it would still be useful. Everything else is supporting detail.

Flag approaches to limits, not just breaches

A weighting at twenty-three percent against a twenty-five percent cap is worth a sentence. Reporting only breaches trains the board to expect silence until something is already wrong, which makes the eventual flag look like a failure rather than a process working.

Say what the numbers are not

One line is enough: that these are management figures from a custodian export dated whenever, not a valuation prepared for the accounts. It costs a sentence and prevents a category of misunderstanding that is tedious to unwind later.

Keep the rationale nearby

If a position has been questioned before, put the reason next to it rather than waiting to be asked again. Boards ask the same question until they get an answer they can remember.

Same shape every period

A section that keeps its structure is one a reader can skim and still absorb. Reordering it each quarter forces a full read every time and makes period-on-period comparison harder than it needs to be.

title: Who can change the numbers?
content:
When treasury reporting lives in a spreadsheet, the controls around it are usually weaker than the controls around the transactions it describes. That gap is worth examining.

The spreadsheet problem

A workbook that produces the holdings schedule typically sits on a shared drive. Several people can edit it. Formulas can be overwritten by anyone who pastes values into the wrong range. There is often no record of who changed what, and the version that reaches the board is whichever copy was attached to the email.

None of that is anybody's fault. It is the default behaviour of the tool.

What good looks like

  • Figures derive from a source file rather than being typed
  • The source file comes from the custodian, not from a person
  • It is obvious which file a given statement was built from
  • Removing or replacing data is deliberate and attributable

The principle is simply that the report should be reproducible. Given the same input file, anyone should get the same statement.

Access is not the same as integrity

Restricting who can open the report is useful but secondary. The more important question is whether the numbers can be altered without that being evident. A read-protected spreadsheet with hand-typed figures is worse than an openly shared report generated from a file nobody edited.

Credentials are a separate matter

A reporting tool should not hold logins to the accounts it reports on. If it does, the blast radius of a compromise stops being a report and starts being the holdings themselves. Working from an exported file keeps those concerns apart.

PortfolioHQ derives every figure from the uploaded file, never asks for custodian or bank credentials, and lets an uploaded book be deleted by the people who put it there.
